# Preparations

Load the necessary libraries

```{r}
#| label: libraries
#| output: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| cache: false

library(gbm)         #for gradient boosted models
library(car)
library(dismo)
library(pdp)
library(ggfortify)
library(randomForest)
library(tidyverse)
library(gridExtra)
library(patchwork)
library(easystats)
```

# Scenario

@Loyn-1987-1987 modelled the abundance of forest birds with six predictor
variables (patch area, distance to nearest patch, distance to nearest
larger patch, grazing intensity, altitude and years since the patch had
been isolated).

![Regent honeyeater](../resources/regent_honeyeater_small.jpg){#fig-honeyeater width="165" height="240"}


ABUND   DIST   LDIST   AREA   GRAZE   ALT   YR.ISOL
------- ------ ------- ------ ------- ----- ---------
..      ..     ..      ..     ..      ..    ..

: Format of loyn.csv data file {#tbl-loyn .table-condensed}

------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
**ABUND**     Abundance of forest birds in patch- response variable
**DIST**      Distance to nearest patch - predictor variable
**LDIST**     Distance to nearest larger patch - predictor variable
**AREA**      Size of the patch - predictor variable
**GRAZE**     Grazing intensity (1 to 5, representing light to heavy) - predictor variable
**ALT**       Altitude - predictor variable
**YR.ISOL**   Number of years since the patch was isolated - predictor variable
------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

: Description of the variables in the loyn data file {#tbl-loyn1 .table-condensed}

The aim of the analysis is to investigate the effects of a range of
predictors on the abundance of forest birds.

We have previously analysed these data in [Example
4](glm_example4.html) and the Bayesian version ([Example
4](bglm_example4.html)). On those occasions, we used a multiple linear
model with scaled predictors (some of which were also log-transformed)
against a lognormal distribution.

On this occassion we will take a different approach. We will use
regression trees in order to explore which variables might be
"important" drivers of bird abundances and the possible nature of any
relationships and interactions. Such an analysis might help refine
sensible candidate models to explore via linear modelling, yet might
also serve as either an analysis in its own right

# Read in the data

```{r readData, results='markdown', eval=TRUE}
loyn <- read_csv('../data/loyn.csv', trim_ws=TRUE)
glimpse(loyn)
```

# Prep data
```{r}
#| label: prep data
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#declare categorical variables
loyn <- loyn |> 
  mutate(
    fGRAZE = factor(GRAZE)
  )

```

# Exploratory data analysis 
```{r}
#| label: scatterplot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#put response first
scatterplotMatrix(~ABUND+AREA+YR.ISOL+DIST+LDIST+fGRAZE+ALT, data = loyn,
                  diagonal = list(method = 'boxplot'))

#monotonic trends = 1, 1, 1, 0, -1, 1
```


# Fit the model
```{r}
#| label: fit model
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#all predictors are additive, no interactions because gbm automatically will include interactions
loyn_gbm <- gbm(ABUND ~ AREA + YR.ISOL + DIST + LDIST + fGRAZE + ALT,
                  data = loyn,
                  distribution = "gaussian", #loss function
                  n.trees = 10000, #a good starting point
                  var.monotone = c(1, 1, 1, 0, -1, 1), #monotonic trends
                  interaction.depth = 5, #how many splits does each tree have (typically 5, 7, or 9)
                  shrinkage = 0.001, #learning rate, only going to retain 1% in memory
                  bag.fraction = 0.5, #50% of data are in and 50% are out for testing at tree level
                  train.fraction = 1, #determines how much is completely withheld and never seen by the model for training (1 = none withheld)
                  n.minobsinnode = 10, #node cannot have less than 10 data points
                  cv.folds = 10 #how many times should each tree be repeated
                  )

(best.iter <- gbm::gbm.perf(loyn_gbm, method = 'cv'))
#5337 trees!
```

# Explore relative influence
```{r}
#| label: relative influence
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

summary(loyn_gbm, n.trees = best.iter)
100/6 #16.67
#AREA and fGRAZE are the most important
```

# Explore partial effects
```{r}
#| label: partial effects plot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

attr(loyn_gbm$Terms, "term.labels")

plot(loyn_gbm, 1, n.tree = best.iter)
#as reef complexity increases, fish richness increases

plot(loyn_gbm, 5, n.tree = best.iter)
#as octocoral height increases, fish richness increases and then decreases

#a nicer way to plot these
loyn_gbm |> 
  pdp::partial(pred.var = 'AREA',
               n.trees = best.iter,
               type = "regression",
               recursive = FALSE,
               ice = TRUE,
               inv.link = NULL, #set to null because gaussian
               grid.resolution = 1000) |> #increase resolution to 1000
  autoplot() +
  scale_x_log10() 

loyn_gbm |> 
  pdp::partial(pred.var = 'fGRAZE',
               n.trees = best.iter,
               type = "regression", 
               recursive = FALSE,
               ice = TRUE,
               inv.link = NULL #set to null because gaussian
              ) |> 
  autoplot() 
  
```

# Tuning


# Bootstrapping
```{r}
#| label: bootstrapping
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#goal is to create a partial plot for AREA

#Create 2 lists:
 # - relative_influence_list
 # - prediction_list

#Need to create newdata (dataset for predictions)

#Step 1: Resample the data
#Step 2. Fit a tree
#Step 3. Cross validation (figure out optimal number of trees)
#Step 4. Calculate relative influence (how important was each predictor)
#Step 5. Predict

#Compile relative influence -> plot
#Compile predictions -> plot

#and we want to do this multiple times (10x)
#need to create a loop

nBoot <- 10 #number of bootstraps
rel_inf_list <- vector("list", nBoot) #empty list with 10 spaces
pred_list <- vector("list", nBoot)
newdata <- with(loyn, data.frame(
  AREA = seq(min(AREA), 
             max(AREA), len = 100), 
  YR.ISOL = mean(YR.ISOL),
  DIST = mean(DIST),
  LDIST = mean(LDIST),
  ALT = mean(ALT))) |> 
  crossing(fGRAZE = levels(loyn$fGRAZE))

#could do log min AREA and log max AREA and then at the end of this section
#use mutate() to get log AREA back to AREA for predictions\
                      

for (i in 1:nBoot) {
  print(paste("Bootstrap no.", i))
  
  dat <- loyn |> 
    sample_n(size = n(), replace = TRUE)
  
  mod_gbm <- gbm(ABUND ~ AREA + YR.ISOL + DIST + LDIST + fGRAZE + ALT,
                  data = dat,
                  distribution = "gaussian", 
                  n.trees = 10000, 
                  var.monotone = c(1, 1, 1, 0, -1, 1), 
                  interaction.depth = 5, 
                  shrinkage = 0.001, 
                  bag.fraction = 0.5, 
                  train.fraction = 1, 
                  n.minobsinnode = 10, 
                  cv.folds = 10
                  )
  
  best.iter <- gbm::gbm.perf(mod_gbm, method = 'cv')
  
  rel_inf_list[[i]] <- summary(mod_gbm, Boot = i, n.trees = best.iter)
  
  fit <- predict(mod_gbm, newdata = newdata, n.trees = best.iter)
  pred_list[[i]] <- data.frame(newdata, Fit = fit, Boot = i)
  
}

#check
str(rel_inf_list)

#compile relative influences and make a plot
rel_inf <- do.call("rbind", rel_inf_list) #do this, on this (aka take list and bind all the shelves into one)
head(rel_inf)

#rel_inf |> 
#  group_by(var) |> 
#  posterior::summarise_draws(median, HDInterval::hdi)

rel_inf |> 
  group_by(var) |> 
  summarise(median = median(rel.inf), lower = HDInterval::hdi(rel.inf)[1], upper = HDInterval::hdi(rel.inf)[2])

#plot of medians and relative importance
g1 <- rel_inf |> 
  group_by(var) |> 
  summarise(median = median(rel.inf), 
            lower = HDInterval::hdi(rel.inf)[1], 
            upper = HDInterval::hdi(rel.inf)[2]) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = median, y = reorder(var, median))) + #orders variables by median
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 16.66, linetype = "dashed")
g1

#plot with uncertainty
pred <- do.call("rbind", pred_list)
#Fit is on a log scale though so we need to back transform
pred <- pred |> 
  #mutate(Fit = exp(Fit)) |> 
  group_by(fGRAZE, AREA) |> 
  tidybayes::median_hdci(Fit) #or use summarise_draws
pred

g2 <- pred |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = Fit, x = log(AREA), fill = fGRAZE)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower, ymax = .upper), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(color = fGRAZE))
g2

g2 | g1 #two plots side by side

g1 + patchwork::inset_element(g2, left = 0.4, bottom = 0.01, right = 1, top = 0.4) & theme_classic()

g2 + patchwork::inset_element(g1, left = 0.01, bottom = 0.01, right = 0.5, top = 0.35) & theme_classic()

```
